checks.about: Every board player is on their team's latest roster landing for the league's latest roster season: no retired, released or waived players.
checks.name: assert_board_rostered

checks.about: Every board row has played games behind its projection, season weights that with the replacement-level prior add up to one, a multiplier and a rest-of-season factor between 0 and 1, a games share between 0 and 1, and season and rest-of-season values no larger in magnitude than the values they scale.
checks.name: assert_board_values_sane

checks.about: Basketball arithmetic on every player-game that was played: PTS = 2*FGM + FG3M + FTM, FGM <= FGA, FG3M <= FGM, FG3A <= FGA, FTM <= FTA, REB = OREB + DREB. A counting stat that is null on a played row fails too: a comparison with a null operand is never true, so without this a source that renamed or dropped a column would pass every arithmetic check while the board's values moved (#383).
checks.name: assert_box_arithmetic

checks.about: The player rows of a team-game add up to the team row for every counting stat except turnovers: the team total includes team turnovers (shot-clock and 8-second violations, inbound violations) that belong to no player, so turnovers are checked separately (warn_team_turnovers).
checks.name: assert_box_closure

checks.about: Every final regular-season or playoff game on the schedule that finished more than a day ago has a box score and play-by-play in gold. Preseason, All-Star, play-in and tournament finals are on the schedule but outside what the ingestors fetch (SPEC.md scope), so they are not counted as missing.  A season a Backfill run is still landing is left out until it finishes (#420): the build passes the league-seasons of the unfinished Backfill runs as var backfilling (["nba:2023-24", ...], ops.backfilling), and the first build after the backfill judges the season again.
checks.name: assert_completeness

checks.about: In season, a core feed (ops.feed_freshness.is_core: the schedule, the game log, box scores, play-by-play, shot charts, rosters, ESPN scoreboards) stale by more than two days past its allowance blocks the publish: the board would otherwise go live on last week's games or rosters while looking current. warn_stale_feeds flags the first stale day of every feed.
checks.name: assert_core_feeds_fresh

checks.about: Every player has exactly one current stint in dim_player: one row with is_current and one with valid_to null, the same row. The board, the streamers and the status models join a player to their current stint and would double the player otherwise.
checks.name: assert_dim_player_one_current_stint

checks.about: A player's stints follow one another: each ends the day before the next begins and only the last is open. A game joined to the stint whose dates contain it would otherwise fan out.
checks.name: assert_dim_player_stints_do_not_overlap

checks.about: In season, the latest game in gold is within 36 hours of the last completed scheduled game. Out of season (no completed scheduled game in the last 14 days) there is nothing to check.
checks.name: assert_freshness_in_season

checks.about: One value scale (#767, ADR 0019). Fails on any of: game_mean     a player's mean regular-season game value is not their season z_total (the scale is linear in a game's numbers, so the two are the same figure) replacement   the board's replacement band (the `teams` players after the pool, by value) does not average zero: value is above replacement level playoff_game  a playoff or play-in game is valued (fantasy windows are the regular season)
checks.name: assert_one_value_scale

checks.about: Projected minutes are the season-weighted figure, or in season a blend of it with the last five games (var fantasy_recent_minutes): never outside the two once the return ramp's cut (var fantasy_return_ramp) is taken back out. The ramp keeps between 1 - max_cut and all of them.
checks.name: assert_projected_minutes_blend

checks.about: The chaos switch: `--vars '{chaos: true}'` makes this error-severity check fail on purpose, so the publish gate and the incident path can be exercised end to end on demand.
checks.name: chaos_deliberate_failure

checks.about: Days the board ledger (fct_board_history) should hold a snapshot for but does not: every Eastern date in the last 45 days, from the league's first snapshot on, while the league was playing (a regular-season, play-in or playoff game within three days either side), with no row. A failed nightly build leaves exactly such a hole, and the ledger is the only history of the newer signals; the runbook ("Fill a hole in the board ledger") says how to put the day back from a kept build. The 45-day window is what the kept builds can still fill with margin to notice; an older hole is history.
checks.name: warn_board_history_gaps

checks.about: At least 99% of a season's played player-games are matched to ESPN through the crosswalk (SPEC.md phase 4). The league lists inactive players with a line of zeros that ESPN does not carry, so the rate is judged over players who were on the floor. Seasons with fewer than 100 played player-games are too small to judge.
checks.name: warn_crosswalk_coverage

checks.about: Made field goals in play-by-play per player-game equal FGM in the box score.
checks.name: warn_event_box_agreement

checks.about: Lines inside plausible bounds for professional basketball: totals between 100 and 300 points, spreads under 40, both sides implied to score, and the two implied scores adding up to the total.
checks.name: warn_game_line_sanity

checks.about: An endpoint whose latest run landed a payload count per window day more than three spreads from the median of its trailing 14 runs (ops.ingest_endpoint_volume, #398). The source-level check (warn_ingest_volume_anomaly) sums a source's endpoints, so one endpoint that stops landing moves the total by a few percent and never warns there.
checks.name: warn_ingest_endpoint_volume_anomaly

checks.about: The latest run per source and league landed a payload count per window day within 3 MAD of the median of the trailing 14 runs (only once there are at least 5 earlier runs to compare with). Full-refresh and backfill runs (explicit windows longer than 10 days) are left out.  A run is judged whole (#393): the stats job logs one record per pass (the regular season, then the playoffs), so its last record was a playoffs pass that found no games, 37 payloads against a median of 185. The passes of a run are summed, the count is taken per day of the run's window (a one-day run and a seven-day run are not compared alike), and the spread is floored at a tenth of the median or two payloads a day, so a source that lands nearly the same count every day does not warn on a difference of a few payloads.
checks.name: warn_ingest_volume_anomaly

checks.about: The players on the latest injury report linked to a league player id reach the good bound of vars.quality_thresholds.listing_links, the one the data-quality notebook grades against; the rest are usually players on two-way or developmental deals missing from both rosters.
checks.name: warn_injury_links

checks.about: A season's actions with five players a side on the floor reach the good bound of vars.quality_thresholds.lineup_complete (90%). Period starters after the first period are inferred, so a player who plays a whole period without an action or a substitution is missed; a drop below it means the substitution format changed.
checks.name: warn_lineup_completeness

checks.about: Player minutes per team-game add up to the team minutes (200 WNBA / 240 NBA, +25 per overtime) within one minute.
checks.name: warn_minutes_closure

checks.about: Players on the league's newest injury report, for upcoming games, that could not be linked to a league player id (by name within the team). A few two-way or newly signed players are expected; more means a team name or a name form the link does not handle.
checks.name: warn_official_injury_links

checks.about: Of the player-games the league and ESPN both report, at most 0.5% may disagree beyond rounding (vars.quality_thresholds.conflict_rate, the good bound; the data-quality notebook grades against the same pair). A season with fewer than 100 matched player-games is too small to judge (#392).
checks.name: warn_reconciliation_conflicts

checks.about: Court coordinates inside the half court (tenths of a foot from the basket) and the three-point flag consistent with distance: a three is at least 21 feet out, a two at most 24.
checks.name: warn_shot_location_sanity

checks.about: Sleeper's trending players on an NBA team that could not be linked to a current league player (by name, birth date and team). A free agent has no team in Sleeper's directory and is left out; more than a few unlinked means a name form the match does not handle.
checks.name: warn_sleeper_links

checks.about: Source feeds that should be landing while the league is playing but have not landed within their expected age (ops.feed_freshness), or have never landed at all in season. A stopped feed keeps its last snapshot in silver and gold, where it would otherwise look current.
checks.name: warn_stale_feeds

checks.about: Team turnovers are the players' turnovers plus team turnovers (no player charged), so the team figure must be at least the players' sum and at most vars.quality_thresholds .team_turnovers_max above it (ADR 0003).
checks.name: warn_team_turnovers

checks.about: Arena cities in the schedule that the venues seed cannot place: their games get no travel or altitude context until the city is added to seeds/venues.csv.
checks.name: warn_venue_cities

conventions.name: dates
conventions.rule: A `*_date` column (and `date_day`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, `week_start`) is the Eastern game date: the day the league counts the game on, which is the day it is played in the US. A UTC date says so (`*_date_utc`); bronze keeps a source's own field names, so ESPN's `event_date` there is the tip-off time as text.

conventions.name: instants
conventions.rule: A `*_at` or `*_datetime_utc` column is an instant, in UTC unless its `tz` badge says otherwise (the official injury reports are published in Eastern time and kept so). Every timestamp column carries `tz`.

conventions.name: units
conventions.rule: Minutes are minutes, distances miles (`*_miles_travelled`), heights inches, weights pounds, percentages ratios from 0 to 1 (`*_pct`), latencies milliseconds (`*_ms`); a `*_pg` column is per game played. A `unit` badge says so where the name alone would not.

conventions.name: nulls
conventions.rule: Null means not known or not applicable, never zero; a `null_when` badge says the condition where it is by design (a listing without a return date, a game without a line).

models.description: The five players on the floor for each side at every play-by-play action (substitution intervals; period starters inferred after the first period). Incremental by game: a game's lineups are recomputed and its rows replaced when its play-by-play or its box score lands again.
models.name: event_lineups
notes: The five players on the floor for each team at every play-by-play action.

The league's play-by-play names only the player leaving on a substitution ("SUB: Key FOR Fagbenle", with the leaving player's id); the player coming on is matched by surname to the game's box score for that team. When two teammates share a surname the feed adds the start of the given name ("SUB: K. Mitchell FOR T. Mitchell", "SUB: Jay. Williams FOR Mitchell"), which must match the given name too; names the feed writes in the other order ("Xu" for Han Xu) match by given name, and a name with more words ("J.J. Redick") by its last word. A player's time on the floor is a set of intervals within a period: a period starter is on from the start, a substitution in opens an interval and one out closes it; the action that is the substitution belongs to the lineup before it. Order is the game clock within the period, with the action number only breaking ties: the feed logs some substitutions late, so action numbers alone are not chronological.

Period starters: period 1 from the box score (starters carry a position). Later periods are inferred: a player is on at the start of a period when, in that period, their first substitution is out, or they record an action before any substitution in. A player who plays a whole period without an action or a substitution is not seen; lineup_complete (five a side) is false for those actions, and the share of complete lineups is checked per season.

Incremental by game (dbt/macros/incremental.sql): a game's lineups are recomputed, and its rows replaced, when its play-by-play or its box score landed on or after the newest landing in the table; _ingest_date is the newer of the two landings a game was built from.

unit_tests.description: Teammates who share a surname are told apart by the start of the given name ("K. Mitchell", "Jal. Williams") or by a suffix ("Carter Jr." is not Carter); a surname that has since gained a hyphenated part ("Laney", now "Laney-Hamilton") still matches; the substitution belongs to the lineup before it. The row's _ingest_date is the newer of the play-by-play's and the box score's landing.
unit_tests.name: event_lineups_matches_abbreviated_given_names

Incremental by game: a game's rows are recomputed and replaced when a landing of it is new (on or after the table's newest); games nothing landed for are not read (ADR 0004, 2026-11-01 addendum).
models.name: events
notes: One row per play-by-play action, typed.

A play-by-play landing is one whole game (its request key is the game id), so the newest landing of a game is the game: an action a corrected feed no longer carries is not kept from an older landing. Incremental by game (dbt/macros/incremental.sql): a run reads only the landings of the games whose play-by-play landed on or after the newest landing in the table, and replaces those games' rows; the games nothing landed for are not read.

unit_tests.description: The table holds G1 and G2 from a landing on the 20th and G0 from the 21st, its newest. On the 22nd G1's play-by-play lands again, corrected and one action fewer, and G3 lands for the first time. The run recomputes G1 from its newest landing alone (the dropped action is not kept from the 20th's landing; the pre-hook, which a unit test does not run, has deleted its old rows), G3 as new, and G0 unchanged (the newest landing day is always redone). G2 is not read at all.
unit_tests.name: events_recomputes_only_the_games_that_landed_again

notes: One row per league, game and official: who officiated each game, and who is assigned to the games of the day.

Two sources. ESPN's game summaries list the crew of every played game (three officials, by name, in an order, each called "Referee"); they reach the league game id through game_xwalk. The leagues' assignments page (official.nba.com) names each of the day's crews by role (crew chief, referee, umpire, and sometimes an alternate) for games it calls "Chicago @ Boston"; a page row reaches the league game id by its date and its two teams, named by city, club or both ("L.A. Lakers"), matched to the teams seed and the schedule's tricodes.

A game ESPN has a crew for takes ESPN's list, with the role from the page where the page named the same official (an official who stepped in has none); a game ESPN has no crew for yet (an upcoming game) takes the page's crew, alternate included. Officials are matched across the two sources by name, reduced to lowercase letters.

unit_tests.description: Last night's game has ESPN's crew (the newest landed summary wins over an older one) and the page's: the crew chief and the referee keep their roles ("JB DeRosa" on the page is "J.B. DeRosa" on ESPN), the official only ESPN lists has none, and the page's umpire who did not work the game is left out. Tonight's games have only the page's crew, alternate included, linked by the date and the teams the page names: "L.A. Lakers" and "LA Clippers" are told apart although both play in Los Angeles. A page row for a game the schedule does not have is left out.
unit_tests.name: game_officials_link_both_sources

notes: Every player-game both sources report, side by side, with the agreement verdict (SPEC.md, "Reconciliation"):

- exact: every compared count agrees and minutes agree within half a minute (ESPN publishes whole minutes, the league publishes mm:ss), or neither source has the player on the floor (the league writes zeros for a player who did not play, ESPN writes nothing);
- minor: the counts agree and minutes differ by at most one minute;
- conflict: anything else.
Only player-games in matched games for crosswalked players appear here; fct_player_game marks the rest 'unverified'.

unit_tests.description: ADR 0005's rules (#397): counts equal and minutes within half a minute is exact, within one minute minor, anything more or any count apart a conflict; a player neither source has on the floor (the league writes zeros, ESPN nothing) is exact.

models.description: Player prop lines from ESPN (DraftKings) and The Odds API: one row per league, game, player, market, source, bookmaker and snapshot, with the prices, the implied probabilities and the over's probability with the vig removed, linked to league player and game ids. Private (ADR 0008).
models.name: player_props
notes: Player prop lines from both sources, one row per league, game, player, market, source, bookmaker and snapshot (one run of the reports ingest, keyed by its Eastern date and hour). Private (ADR 0008): a model input and an analysis aid, never on a public page or in the public JSON, and never a pick.

- Prices. The over and under come as American odds, and each implies a probability: -150 implies 150 / 250 = 0.6, +130 implies 100 / 230. The two add up to more than one, and the excess is the bookmaker's margin (vig). over_prob_no_vig divides it out: over / (over + under).
- Markets. ESPN's prop types and The Odds API's market keys share one set of names: points, rebounds, assists, threes, steals, blocks, turnovers, and the combinations ESPN quotes.

- Games. An ESPN event takes the league game id from the game crosswalk once the game is played. Before then it comes from the schedule: the same two teams (through team_xwalk, either way round) on the same Eastern date. The Odds API names teams in full ("Los Angeles Clippers"). A name links to the league team with that full name or, failing that, the team whose nickname it ends with, the longest nickname winning ("Hornets" over "Nets"). The schedule match then works the same way.

- Players. ESPN athletes link through the player crosswalk. The Odds API gives only the name, which is matched the way transactions and the waiver trend match names: the league name with its suffix kept, or both names without suffixes. A player on one of the game's two teams wins over a namesake elsewhere, then a player on a roster. A name that still matches more than one player is left unlinked.
- Repeated quotes. When a bookmaker quotes one player's market at more than one line in a snapshot, the line with the most even prices is kept: the main line, not an alternate.

unit_tests.description: The Odds API names teams in full: "Los Angeles Clippers" links by its nickname and "Charlotte Hornets" by its full name, not to the Nets whose nickname it also ends with. A player's name links with its suffix kept or dropped; a namesake on one of the game's teams wins, a name unique in the league links on its own, and a tie stays unlinked. Two lines for one player's market keep the one with the most even prices. Each bookmaker keeps its own row.
unit_tests.name: player_props_link_odds_api_teams_and_players_by_name

unit_tests.description: Each price implies a probability (-300 is 0.75, +100 is 0.5); their sum less one is the vig, and the over's share of the sum is its probability with the vig removed. An ESPN event links to the scheduled game with the same two teams on its Eastern date, and an athlete through the player crosswalk; an athlete the crosswalk does not know stays unlinked. A market outside the known set is dropped, and a snapshot taken after the start is not pre-game.
unit_tests.name: player_props_remove_the_vig_and_link_espn_athletes_and_events

models.name: player_xwalk
notes: League stats API player id to ESPN athlete id, one row per matched player (SPEC.md, "Reconciliation"). Three passes over the players who appear in matched games:

1. exact: the same normalised name on the same team in the same game, in either token order ("Xu Han" is "Han Xu"), by the roster's parenthesised nickname ("Asia (AD) Durr" is "AD Durr"), or by first and last token alone ("Cyesha Damian Goree" is "Cyesha Goree"); 2. fuzzy: among players neither pass matched, a name similarity above the engine's threshold within the same team-game, the bar lowered when the rosters give the same birthdate (ADR 0005); 3. override: seeds/player_id_overrides.csv, which beats both.
A pair has to be the best for the stats player and the best for the ESPN athlete. Players left without a pair are listed in player_xwalk_review.

Every model that counts a team's games (remaining, this week, back-to-backs, stakes, travel) reads this instead of unioning the schedule's two sides itself; each keeps its own filters on game type, status and venue.

notes: A daily ledger of the board: what the board said about each player on each Eastern date, kept after the builds that published it roll off. Every build merges today's rows (a later build the same day replaces them), and a full refresh never rebuilds it (full_refresh=false), so the history only grows. It holds the projection and value, and the context the board shows beside the value (availability with the official status and reason, lineups, the ESPN market with its raw shares, stakes, waiver heat, last-ten production, the newest headline flag), so the signals that have only days of history so far can be backtested once they have a season.

models.description: One row per play-by-play action. Incremental by game: a game's rows are replaced when its play-by-play, box score or game record lands again, so a box score that lands after the play-by-play still fills in the lineups and the game date, and an action a re-landed feed no longer carries goes away.
models.name: fct_event
notes: One row per play-by-play action, with the five players on the floor for each side (silver.event_lineups: comma-separated league player ids, sorted; lineup_complete when both sides have five).

Incremental by game, not by the event's landing date: the row also carries the game date from games and the lineups from event_lineups, which come from the box score, and a box score may land a day after the play-by-play (the completeness check tolerates exactly that). A game is recomputed, its rows replaced (dbt/macros/incremental.sql), whenever any of its inputs landed on or after the newest landing already in the table, so a late box score fills in the lineups without a full refresh and an action a re-landed feed no longer carries goes away.

unit_tests.description: Game G1's play-by-play landed on the 20th and was merged without lineups because its box score had not landed; on the 21st other games landed, moving the table's newest landing past G1's. On the 22nd G1's box score and G2's play-by-play land. The next run re-merges G1 (its box score landed on or after the table's newest landing) with its lineups, merges G2 as new, and re-merges G3 unchanged (the newest landing day always is). Keyed on the event's own landing date, G1 would have stayed without lineups until a full refresh.

models.description: Absence spells from the official injury reports, censoring-aware (#768): one row per run of regular-season games a listed player missed, to the next game played. A spell without a return is censored (ongoing, or the season ended first), so its games and days are a lower bound. What the recovery-timeline model (#770) reads.
models.name: fct_injury_spell
notes: Absence spells from the official injury reports, censoring-aware (#768, epic #751): one row per run of regular-season games a listed player missed, from the first listed game missed to the next game the player played. It is the input the recovery-timeline survival model (#770) reads.
- A spell is the listed games a player missed that share the same next played game: listings for consecutive missed games, even with a game between them the report left the player off.

- games_missed counts the team's regular-season games from the first through the last before the return (fct_official_listing's count for the spell's first listing); days_out the days from the first game missed to the return.

- A spell with a return is observed. One without is censored, not short: `ongoing` while the team still has regular-season games to play (the spell was running at the cut, and a point-in-time build cuts it as of its date), `season_end` when the season ended first. Either way games_missed and days_out are what was seen, a lower bound on the spell, and a survival model must treat them so; counting them as finished spells understates long injuries.

- What it was: the first listing's status, the most serious status listed during the spell, and the injury detail of the first listing split into the side (left, right), the body part and the kind (soreness, sprain, strain, fracture, surgery, ...; null when the report says only "injury" or repeats the body part). The league's own reason group says whether it was an injury, rest, personal, a suspension or another absence; a concussion protocol listing is an injury to the head.

unit_tests.description: a misses two listed games (Questionable, then Out, a left ankle sprain) and plays the third: one spell of two games, returned. b misses the last two games played so far and the team has games left: censored, ongoing, two games seen. c misses the last game of a finished season: censored at the season's end, not a one-game injury. d is listed and plays: no spell. e is out resting: an absence, with no body part.
unit_tests.name: injury_spells_are_censoring_aware

models.name: fct_referee_tendency
notes: Official × league-season: the regular-season games an official worked and how those games went against the league-season's average game. A game's figures are both teams' together (fct_team_game): personal fouls, free-throw attempts and points, and the pace of the game (the two teams' average possessions per regulation game). A delta is the official's average game less the league-season's average game; a crew's tendency (mart_schedule_upcoming) averages its officials'.

Season aggregates, not point-in-time: an official's row counts every game of the season, the ones after a given game included. The out-of-sample test of whether a crew's tendency says anything about a player's game (notebook 03, ADR 0003) works from each official's earlier games only. An alternate who did not work the game is not counted.

unit_tests.description: Two regular-season games make the league-season's average game: 38 fouls, 45 free-throw attempts, pace 98 and 210 points. An official who worked only the first, as crew chief, sits 2 fouls, 5 attempts, 2 possessions and 10 points above it; one who worked both sits on it. A preseason game, and an alternate who did not work, count for nothing.
unit_tests.name: referee_tendency_against_the_league_season_average

notes: How many games a listed player then misses, by league, status and reason: the histogram the board's availability multiplier reads (ADR 0003, 2026-11-01 addendum).

One row per league served, status, reason group and number of games missed, with the past listings that missed exactly that many (fct_official_listing). A league reads its own listings once it has calibration_min_listings (300) for the status and reason; until then the NBA's stand in, since the WNBA archive only starts in 2026, and source_league says whose they are. The board joins a listed player to the rows for their league, status and reason, caps each games_missed at the games the team has left and takes the listings-weighted mean; the game context notebook shows the same rows. own_listings is the league's own count for the status and reason, the number the switch is made on.

unit_tests.description: The NBA has two Out listings (0 and 4 games missed) and three Questionable ones (0, 1, 1). The WNBA has one Questionable listing, far short of the 300 the switch needs, so its Questionable rows are the NBA's with source_league nba and own_listings 1; its Out rows are the NBA's too, with no own listings at all. The WNBA has 300 Out-for-rest listings, so those rows are its own. The NBA has no rest listings and the NBA is its own fallback, so it gets no Out-for-rest row.
unit_tests.name: status_calibration_falls_back_to_the_nba_until_a_league_has_enough

notes: The circumstances of each team's games, played and scheduled: days of rest before the game, the second night of a back-to-back, a third game in four nights, the miles travelled from the previous game's city, the time zones crossed, and the altitude of the venue.

The venue is the game's arena city (silver.schedule), placed by the venues seed (latitude, longitude, elevation, standard UTC offset and whether the city keeps daylight saving); a city missing from the seed leaves travel and altitude null and warn_venue_cities lists it. Time zones are counted on the clock in force on the game's date: Arizona, Mexico City and a few overseas venues keep standard time all year, so in summer Phoenix is on Los Angeles time. at_altitude marks a venue 4,000 feet up or more for both teams; visiting_at_altitude marks the team that does not play there at home, the one the thin air is thought to cost. Travel is the great-circle distance between the two venues, so a home stand after a road trip counts the flight home. Only regular-season, play-in, playoff and cup-final games count, and an "if necessary" game is left out until it is confirmed, as is a knockout game whose teams are not decided yet (the schedule lists them as 0).

unit_tests.description: A road trip from Denver to Salt Lake City the next night and on to Los Angeles two nights later: the second game is a back-to-back, visiting at altitude, 370 miles away in the same time zone, the third is the third game in four nights, 581 miles west and one time zone back. An unconfirmed "if necessary" game and a knockout game whose teams are not decided yet (both listed as 0) are left out, and the team they play on the second night sees its opponent on a back-to-back.
unit_tests.name: team_game_context_rest_travel_and_altitude

unit_tests.description: Phoenix keeps standard time all year. A trip from Phoenix to Los Angeles crosses no time zone in July (both on UTC-7) and one in January (UTC-7 to UTC-8).

models.name: fct_walk_year
notes: Who was playing out his contract (#790, for the contract-year study #772): one row per NBA player per regular season he played, with whether it was his walk year.

A season Y was a player's walk year when, between Y's last regular-season game and the next season's first, he signed a standard contract, with a new team or re-signing with his own, in the league's official movement feed (silver.transactions, source nba). Ten-day, two-way, rest-of-season and substitute deals, rookie-scale contracts and extensions do not count: none says a contract ran out.

The flag is hindsight. It rebuilds what was public during Y, an expiring contract, from what happened after it. That is right for measuring the effect, and a point-in-time build cannot know it inside the season, since its transactions stop at the cut. A live flag would need current contract lengths and is built only if the study finds an effect. Noise it does not remove: player options, a free agent who signs only after the next season starts, and a player waived and re-signed in the offseason.

unit_tests.description: a re-signs with his team in July after 2018-19: a walk year. b signs a two-way deal and c an extension that summer: neither says a contract ran out. d signs a standard contract during the season and e only after the next season began: not this season's walk year. f did not play the season and gets no row.
unit_tests.name: a_walk_year_is_a_standard_signing_in_the_offseason_after

models.description: The value scale (#767, ADR 0019): per league and season, the fantasy league's pool (teams x roster spots, chosen in two passes) and its category means, spreads and replacement level. The board's projection sets it for the season the board values, the regular-season lines for every other season. Every value on the site is scored on it.
models.name: int_value_scale
notes: The value scale (#767, ADR 0019): one row per league and season with the pool's category means and spreads, its shooting percentages, the spread of the shooting impact, and each category's replacement level. Every value on the site is measured on it (macros/value_scale.sql), so a player's season, last twenty and ten games, single games and projection are all value per game above the league's replacement level, in the same units.

One pool definition for every season: the fantasy league's pool_size players (teams x roster spots, the `fantasy` var), chosen in two passes. Pass zero orders by minutes; pass one standardises over its pool and ranks by value; pass two standardises over pass one's pool, so the means and spreads describe the players a league actually rosters. Replacement level is the average category score of the next `teams` players. The pool is never so large that no one is left to set replacement level.

The lines are the board's projection for the season it values (mart_player_projection), and the regular-season lines for every other season (int_player_window_lines). A projection is already a per-game expectation shrunk toward replacement level, so it ranks as it stands. A past season's line is not, so it is shrunk the same way before it ranks or sets replacement level: by prior_games games (the `fantasy` var) at the level of the players just outside the pool by minutes, the line the projection's own prior comes from. A player with a few big or a few awful games then lands near replacement level rather than in the pool or the replacement band. Pass zero orders a projection by minutes per game and a past season by its total minutes.

unit_tests.description: Thirty projected players in a two-team, five-spot league (pool of ten, replacement level the next two; #767). Only points vary. Minutes equal points except for two players: p05 scores like a pool player but plays five minutes, p11 plays forty but scores like a replacement. Pass one, which pools by minutes, takes p11 and not p05 (a points mean of 19.5); pass two pools by pass-one value, so the pool is the ten highest scorers, p05 in and p11 out, and the scale's points mean is theirs, 20. A past season's line with no projection is the realized season's own scale; a playoff line never reaches it (int_player_window_lines).
unit_tests.name: value_scale_pool_is_chosen_in_two_passes

unit_tests.description: A past season's lines are shrunk by prior_games games at the level of the players just outside the pool by minutes before they rank (#767). Ten regulars play 70 games at 30 down to 12 points; two call-ups play two scoreless games. Pool of four (two teams, two spots). Ranked by season total, the call-ups' two awful games (z about -10 each, -21 in total) would beat the 70 games of a regular a little below the pool mean (-27) and take two pool places, a points mean of 14.5. Shrunk, they sit near the bottom, and the pool is the four best regulars, a mean of 27.
unit_tests.name: value_scale_shrinks_a_past_season_before_it_ranks

models.description: The board, one row per rostered player per league: category values above replacement from the projected line, recent form, the per-game line, injury status and rest-of-season scaling.
models.name: mart_board
notes: The draft and in-season board: one row per rostered player per league.

Value is scored once, on each player's projected per-game line (mart_player_projection: per-minute production times projected minutes), on the season's value scale (int_value_scale, ADR 0019): the pool_size players a league rosters, chosen in two passes over the projected lines, set each category's mean and spread. Counting categories are z-scores of the projected per-game numbers (turnovers negative); percentages are makes above the pool's percentage on the attempts, standardised over the pool. The season, last twenty and last ten columns are on the same scale (mart_category_zscores), so they compare directly with the value.

Every category then has replacement level subtracted: the average category score of the next `teams` players after the pool. Zero is a freely available player, so the nine values sum to value per game above replacement (value_per_game) and a punt build is the sum without the punted columns. value_total counts games: value per game times the projected share of team games the player plays (games_share), since a missed game is filled by a replacement-level player; a value below replacement is left as it is.

Alongside the value the row carries the current season's z-scores over the whole season and the last twenty and ten games, the per-game line, the projected line itself, and the player's age and rookie status from the roster, so the app can rank on recent form or raw production too and filter the way a fantasy manager does.

Rest of season counts regular-season games only, the games fantasy leagues score. While some remain, ros_factor is the team's remaining share of its regular season times the availability multiplier, the share of those games the player is expected to play given the current status. The games a listed player is expected to miss are calibrated on history (fct_official_listing): the average, over past injury listings with the same status, of the games the player then missed, capped at the games the team has left, with the same reason (an official Out for rest is averaged over rest listings, not injuries). The status is the official report's for the next game, else ESPN's listing in the report's words (day-to-day reads as questionable); the history is fct_status_calibration's histogram, the league's own listings once it has 300 for the status and reason, else the NBA's. ESPN's expected return date, when given for a player ruled out, counts the games before it instead, and a note that the player is out for the season counts them all. Without any history the old charges apply (out: every game; doubtful 0.75 of a game, questionable 0.5, day-to-day 0.25). value_rest_of_season scales value above replacement by it; a value below replacement is left as it is, since a missing game from a player not worth rostering costs nothing. Once the regular season is over (playoffs or the off-season) season_complete is true and ros_factor is 1. A regular (fantasy_rest_risk.min_minutes projected) on a team with nothing left to play for (fct_team_stakes.rest_risk) is expected to sit out fantasy_rest_risk.extra_sit_out more of the games left, measured point in time in notebook 03 (#494): the multiplier keeps the rest. games_next_7 counts playoff games too.

unit_tests.description: Team A has four regular-season games left; team B has played its last. One player per branch of the availability multiplier: a (team B, nothing left) 1.0 and a rest-of-season factor of 0, the team's season being over; b (out, back on the 13th) misses the one game before that date, 0.75; c (out for the season) 0; d (officially questionable with an injury, two past questionable listings that cost one and three games) the calibrated average of two games, 0.5; e (no status) 1.0; f (out, no return date, no history) 0; g (doubtful, no history) the old charge of 0.75 of a game, 0.8125; h (officially questionable for rest, a reason with no history) the old charge of half a game, 0.875; i (officially probable, whose one past listing cost ten games) the calibrated games capped at the four the team has left, 0; j (officially available after a rest listing, still day-to-day on ESPN) reads as probable for rest, whose one past listing cost no games, 1.0 and no status shown, as Streamers shows it (#388); k (no status, a regular of 30 projected minutes on team A, which has nothing left to play for) sits out 0.29 more of the games left, 0.71 (#494), while the other team A players, projected at no minutes, are not regulars. b (listed out) and e (not listed) both have a projected share of 0.6 that is 0.9 without the absence they are on: b's share is 0.9, because his availability already charges that absence, and e's stays 0.6 (#690). Every projected line is zero, so value is zero and the factors are exact.
unit_tests.name: board_availability_follows_the_status

unit_tests.description: The NBA lists two games per team as placeholders until the Cup's group stage ends, so its schedule says 80 games; with regular_season_games set (10 here, for a short schedule) the NBA team that has played three of its ten has seven left whatever is scheduled, and its rest-of-season factor is 7/10. The WNBA, not listed, counts its schedule: two played, six scheduled, 6/8 (#386).
unit_tests.name: board_counts_a_fixed_season_length_where_the_schedule_cannot

unit_tests.description: Thirty players on one team in a two-team, five-spot league (pool of ten). The board scores each projected line on the season's value scale (int_value_scale, whose two-pass pool is pinned by value_scale_pool_is_chosen_in_two_passes): only points vary, so value is the points z-score, and the pool is the ten the scale values most, p05 (five minutes) in and p11 (forty minutes, a replacement's points) out. rank_total follows value, equal points broken by player id.
unit_tests.name: board_pool_is_chosen_in_two_passes

Shooting is makes above the pool's percentage on the attempts: 6 of 10 against a pool's 50% is one make over, a spread of 2 makes it 0.5.

models.description: One projected per-game line per player on a current roster: per-minute production from the current season and the two before, weighted by minutes times recency, times projected minutes, each from a replacement-level prior; in season, projected minutes blend with the last five games (fantasy_recent_minutes) and are cut for a player still out or just back from an absence (fantasy_return_ramp).
models.name: mart_player_projection
notes: One projected line per player on a current roster: what the board scores.
The projection separates how much a player plays from what they do while playing:

- Minutes per game: each season's minutes per game counted by games played times a minutes recency weight (per league, var fantasy.<league>.minutes_recency), so a change of role in the current season shows within a few games where the league's roles move a lot (WNBA). A past season spent mostly on another team counts for var fantasy_team_change (0.25) of its minutes weight: the role was a different team's. Per-minute production carries over. In season, with five or more games for the current team, the figure is blended with the player's last five games at var fantasy_recent_minutes (0.5), so a role change shows at once.

- Return ramp: in season, for a player with five or more games this season who is still out, or just back, after three or more straight games of the current team missed, minutes per game are cut by 1% per game of that absence (at most 50%) while the player is out, half that after the first game back and none from the second (var fantasy_return_ramp). Players come back on reduced minutes, and the last five games only show it once they have been played. The team's games count from the player's first game for it this season, or from its first game when it was their main team last season, so an injury carried over from last season counts.

- Production per minute: each season's totals over its minutes, counted by minutes played times the production recency weight (var fantasy_recency: 1.0, 0.25, 0.08). A season of 60 games at 8 minutes counts for far less than 60 games at 34.
- Per-game line: production per minute times projected minutes.
- Seasons are regular-season lines (int_player_window_lines, #767): playoff games are not fantasy games and do not move a player's minutes or production.

- Games share (durability): the share of their team's regular-season games a player played in the seasons they appeared in, by the same recency, regressed toward a typical share by durability_games games (var fantasy.<league>.durability_games, fantasy_durability). Regular season only: playoff games would make every team that missed the playoffs look as if its players sat out.

Every projection also starts from prior_games games of a replacement-level player (var fantasy: 3 NBA, 5 WNBA), at that player's minutes and per-minute production, so a short sample moves a projection only part of the way and a missing season adds nothing. All settings were chosen by backtest (ADR 0003).

The replacement-level line is the average line of the players just outside a fantasy league's rosters by total minutes (ranks pool_size + 1 to pool_size + teams) in the league's latest complete regular season.

Current roster: the player is on their team's latest roster landing for the league's latest roster season. A player waived or released drops off with the next landing, and a retired player is on no roster at all, so neither is projected. Only players with at least one game in the three seasons are projected.

unit_tests.description: Team A has played ten games. p1 missed five in a row (one listed as did not play) and has played one game back: the cut of 0.125 a game missed reaches the 0.5 cap and is halved, keeping 0.75 of the minutes. p2 has missed the last three: still out, 0.625 kept. p3 missed two, too few to count. p4, on team A last season, missed the first three games and has played seven since: the absence is reported but no longer cuts. p5 joined the team at its sixth game, which is no absence. p6 has missed six after four games: under five games this season, so no cut. Projected minutes are the blended minutes (30) times the share kept.
unit_tests.name: projection_return_ramp_cuts_minutes_after_an_absence

models.description: Regular-season and playoff games not yet final in the next fourteen days, unconfirmed if-necessary games left out, with matchup values, betting lines, rest and travel.
models.name: mart_schedule_upcoming
notes: The games of the next fourteen days per league, for the Streamers week grid and the board's games-next-seven column. Only regular-season and playoff games count, and an "if necessary" playoff game is left out until it is confirmed (the league stops flagging it once it is on).

Each side of a game carries a matchup value: how much a player's value per game moves with the opponent's defence and the game's expected pace, from replaying past seasons (ADR 0003: one standard deviation of opponent defence is worth about 0.2 value per game in the NBA, against a game-to-game swing of about 2.5; var fantasy_matchup). A team's defensive rating and pace blend this season to date with last season, last season counting as prior_games games, so early in a season (and for a reworked roster) the current games take over as they accumulate; early on, last season's team defence was the better guide. Ratings are standardised over the league's teams. A player's past results against an opponent predicted nothing (correlation 0.00 to 0.04) and are not used.

Each game also carries its betting line where the sportsbooks have posted one (silver game_lines): the home spread, the over/under, and the points each side is implied to score. The line is shown alongside the matchup value and does not change it until a backtest says it adds to it.

Once the leagues post the day's referee assignments, a game carries its crew chief and the crew's tendency (fct_referee_tendency): the average, over the crew chief, referee and umpire, of each official's fouls, free-throw attempts and pace against the league average game, over this season and last, each official's figure shrunk toward zero as if they had also worked 20 average games. It is context only and does not change the value (ADR 0003).

unit_tests.description: The games ahead are every game a team plays (#391): the regular season, the play-in and the playoffs. The preseason and the in-season cup's final, which no fantasy league counts, are left out, as is a game already final.
unit_tests.name: schedule_upcoming_counts_the_play_in

unit_tests.description: Tonight's game has its crew from the assignments page. The crew chief worked 20 games this season and last, 2 free-throw attempts and 1 possession above the league's average game, so shrunk as if 20 average games more, 1 and 0.5; the referee worked 60 games last season 4 attempts below and at the average pace (-3 and 0; the season before does not count); the umpire worked 20 games 1 attempt and 2 possessions above (0.5 and 1). The crew sits half an attempt below the average game and half a possession above it. The alternate does not count. A game without a crew yet has none.
unit_tests.name: schedule_upcoming_crew_tendency

models.description: Players with three or more games in the league's current season and a game within 30 days of the league's latest game, with the team's games in the next seven days, the minutes and value trend, recent production and injury status.
models.name: mart_streamers
notes: Streaming candidates: one row per player active in the league's current season, with the team's games over the next seven days, the minutes trend and recent production.
Active means at least three games this season and a game within the last thirty days of the league's season so far, so players from earlier seasons never appear.

The trends compare recent games with a baseline: minutes over the last five games, value over the last ten. The baseline is the player's games this season before the window, blended with the player's latest earlier season (last season, or the one before for a player who missed it) counted as up to 10 games. Early in a season the window is the whole season, so the baseline is last season; late in a season it is mostly this one. A player with neither (a rookie's first games) has no trend rather than a misleading zero.

Each row also carries the last-ten-games z-score per category, for ranking by the categories a manager needs, and the player's board rank and value, for leaving out players a league of a given size has most likely rostered (null for a player not on a current roster). The value baseline uses the season z-score, which includes the window; with few games before the window it is weighted toward last season accordingly. While the league is between seasons the same columns describe who finished the season strongly, and season_complete says so.

notes: How fresh each source feed is, per league: the newest day a payload landed for it and how many days ago that was, against how often the feed should land while the league is playing. A feed that stops keeps its last landing in silver and gold, where it would otherwise look current; warn_stale_feeds reports a stale one. Out of season (no game three days either side of today) a quiet feed is expected. An unchanged payload lands no new file, so the slower feeds get a few days' grace: a roster or a player directory changes some days, not every day.

Minutes equal points except for two players: p05 scores like a pool player but plays five minutes, p11 plays forty but scores like a replacement. Pass one, which pools by minutes, takes p11 and not p05 (a points mean of 19.5); pass two pools by pass-one value, so the pool is the ten highest scorers, p05 in and p11 out, and the scale's points mean is theirs, 20. A past season's line with no projection is the realized season's own scale; a playoff line never reaches it (int_player_window_lines).

Ten regulars play 70 games at 30 down to 12 points; two call-ups play two scoreless games. Pool of four (two teams, two spots). Ranked by season total, the call-ups' two awful games (z about -10 each, -21 in total) would beat the 70 games of a regular a little below the pool mean (-27) and take two pool places, a points mean of 14.5. Shrunk, they sit near the bottom, and the pool is the four best regulars, a mean of 27.

unit_tests.description: Team A has four regular-season games left; team B has played its last. One player per branch of the availability multiplier: a (team B, nothing left) 1.0 and a rest-of-season factor of 0, the team's season being over; b (out, back on the 13th) misses the one game before that date, 0.75; c (out for the season) 0; d (officially questionable with an injury, two past questionable listings that cost one and three games) the calibrated average of two games, 0.5; e (no status) 1.0; f (out, no return date, no history) 0; g (doubtful, no history) the old charge of 0.75 of a game, 0.8125; h (officially questionable for rest, a reason with no history) the old charge of half a game, 0.875; i (officially probable, whose one past listing cost ten games) the calibrated games capped at the four the team has left, 0; j (officially available after a rest listing, still day-to-day on ESPN) reads as probable for rest, whose one past listing cost no games, 1.0 and no status shown, as Streamers shows it (#388); k (no status, a regular of 30 projected minutes on team A, which has nothing left to play for) sits out 0.29 more of the games left, 0.71 (#494), while the other team A players, projected at no minutes, are not regulars. b (listed out) and e (not listed) both have a projected share of 0.6 that is 0.9 without the absence they are on: b's share is 0.9, because his availability already charges that absence, and e's stays 0.6 (#690). Every projected line is zero, so value is zero and the factors are exact.
